sections.collegeNotes:
**Two classification schemes.** Joints are described by what holds them together (**structural**) and by how much they move (**functional**), and the two overlap:

- **Fibrous joints** are connected by dense fibrous connective tissue and are generally **immovable (synarthroses)** — for example, the **sutures** of the skull.
- **Cartilaginous joints** are connected by cartilage and are usually **slightly movable (amphiarthroses)** — for example, the joints between vertebrae (with their discs) and the pubic symphysis.
- **Synovial joints** have a fluid-filled cavity and are **freely movable (diarthroses)** — nearly all the joints of the limbs. These are the joints most people picture and the ones most involved in injury.

**Anatomy of a synovial joint.** Synovial joints share a set of features designed for smooth, protected movement:

- **Articular cartilage** (hyaline) caps the bone ends, reducing friction and absorbing shock.
- A **joint (articular) capsule** encloses the joint; its inner **synovial membrane** secretes **synovial fluid** into the **joint cavity** to lubricate and nourish the cartilage.
- **Ligaments** (bone to bone) reinforce and stabilize the joint.
- Some joints have extra structures: **menisci** (cartilage pads, as in the knee) for cushioning and fit, and **bursae** (fluid-filled sacs) that reduce friction between moving parts.

**Types of synovial joints** allow different motions, including the **ball-and-socket** (shoulder, hip — movement in all directions), **hinge** (elbow, knee — bending in one plane), **pivot** (between the first two neck vertebrae — rotation), **gliding/plane** (between wrist bones — sliding), **saddle** (thumb), and **condylar** (knuckles) joints.

**Common body movements.** Synovial joints produce named movements you'll use constantly in assessment:

- **Flexion / extension:** decreasing / increasing the angle of a joint (bending / straightening the elbow).
- **Abduction / adduction:** moving away from / toward the body's midline (raising the arm sideways / lowering it).
- **Rotation:** turning around an axis (shaking the head "no").
- **Circumduction:** moving a limb in a cone shape (windmilling the arm).
- Specialized moves include **pronation/supination** (turning the palm down/up), **dorsiflexion/plantarflexion** (lifting the foot up / pointing the toes), and **inversion/eversion** (turning the sole inward/outward).

sections.eli10:
### ELI-10 Explains

### Simple idea
Joints are the places where bones meet. Some are locked tight, some barely move, and some — the ones full of slippery fluid — move freely so you can bend, twist, and reach.

### Analogy
Think of different kinds of connections in a toy. Some pieces are **glued together** and don't move at all — that's like the **sutures** in your skull (fibrous joints). Some are joined with a bit of **rubber** so they can wiggle a little — like the cushioned joints in your spine (cartilaginous joints). And some are like **well-oiled hinges and ball-joints** that swing freely — those are your **synovial joints**, like your knees, elbows, shoulders, and hips. The freely moving ones come with built-in grease (**synovial fluid**), smooth caps on the bone ends (**cartilage**), and strong straps (**ligaments**) holding them together.

### What is actually happening
Different synovial joints move in different ways: **ball-and-socket** joints (shoulder, hip) swing in all directions, while **hinge** joints (elbow, knee) mainly bend and straighten. The motions have names nurses use — **flexion** (bending), **extension** (straightening), **abduction** (moving away from the middle), and more. Because these moving joints get so much use, they're where injuries like **sprains** and diseases like **arthritis** (worn or inflamed joints) show up.

### Where the analogy stops
Toy hinges wear out and can't fix themselves, but real joints are living — they make fresh lubricating fluid and can heal minor injuries, though badly worn cartilage (arthritis) doesn't grow back well.

sourceSnapshotMarkdown:
# Joints (Articulations)

## What This Topic Is

A **joint (articulation)** is where two bones meet. This section classifies joints **structurally** (fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial) and **functionally** (immovable, slightly movable, freely movable), details the anatomy of a **synovial joint**, and reviews common **body movements**.

## Why It Matters

Joints make movement possible and are frequent sites of injury and disease — sprains, dislocations, and arthritis. Understanding joint types explains why some joints move freely while others don't, and why synovial joints (the movable ones) are so vulnerable.

## Learning Objectives

- Classify joints **structurally** and **functionally**.
- Describe the anatomy of a **synovial joint**.
- Name types of synovial joints and their motions.
- Define common **body movements** (flexion, extension, etc.).

## Key Terms

- **Joint (articulation)** — the site where bones meet.
- **Fibrous joint** — bones joined by fibrous tissue; usually immovable (e.g., skull sutures).
- **Cartilaginous joint** — bones joined by cartilage; slightly movable (e.g., between vertebrae, pubic symphysis).
- **Synovial joint** — a fluid-filled joint; freely movable (most limb joints).
- **Articular cartilage** — cartilage covering bone ends in a synovial joint.
- **Synovial fluid** — lubricating fluid in the joint cavity.

## Core Explanation

**Two classification schemes.** Joints are described by what holds them together (**structural**) and by how much they move (**functional**), and the two overlap:

- **Fibrous joints** are connected by dense fibrous connective tissue and are generally **immovable (synarthroses)** — for example, the **sutures** of the skull.
- **Cartilaginous joints** are connected by cartilage and are usually **slightly movable (amphiarthroses)** — for example, the joints between vertebrae (with their discs) and the pubic symphysis.
- **Synovial joints** have a fluid-filled cavity and are **freely movable (diarthroses)** — nearly all the joints of the limbs. These are the joints most people picture and the ones most involved in injury.

**Anatomy of a synovial joint.** Synovial joints share a set of features designed for smooth, protected movement:

- **Articular cartilage** (hyaline) caps the bone ends, reducing friction and absorbing shock.
- A **joint (articular) capsule** encloses the joint; its inner **synovial membrane** secretes **synovial fluid** into the **joint cavity** to lubricate and nourish the cartilage.
- **Ligaments** (bone to bone) reinforce and stabilize the joint.
- Some joints have extra structures: **menisci** (cartilage pads, as in the knee) for cushioning and fit, and **bursae** (fluid-filled sacs) that reduce friction between moving parts.

**Types of synovial joints** allow different motions, including the **ball-and-socket** (shoulder, hip — movement in all directions), **hinge** (elbow, knee — bending in one plane), **pivot** (between the first two neck vertebrae — rotation), **gliding/plane** (between wrist bones — sliding), **saddle** (thumb), and **condylar** (knuckles) joints.

**Common body movements.** Synovial joints produce named movements you'll use constantly in assessment:

- **Flexion / extension:** decreasing / increasing the angle of a joint (bending / straightening the elbow).
- **Abduction / adduction:** moving away from / toward the body's midline (raising the arm sideways / lowering it).
- **Rotation:** turning around an axis (shaking the head "no").
- **Circumduction:** moving a limb in a cone shape (windmilling the arm).
- Specialized moves include **pronation/supination** (turning the palm down/up), **dorsiflexion/plantarflexion** (lifting the foot up / pointing the toes), and **inversion/eversion** (turning the sole inward/outward).

## How It Works

Classifying a joint:

1. **What connects the bones?** fibrous, cartilaginous, or synovial (structural).
2. **How much does it move?** immovable, slightly movable, freely movable (functional).
3. **Freely movable?** → it's synovial: expect articular cartilage, a capsule with synovial fluid, and ligaments.
4. **Name the movement** by how the joint angle or position changes (flexion, abduction, rotation, etc.).

## Important Relationships and Comparisons

| Structural type | Functional type | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fibrous | Immovable | Skull sutures |
| Cartilaginous | Slightly movable | Intervertebral joints, pubic symphysis |
| Synovial | Freely movable | Shoulder, hip, knee, elbow |

| Movement | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Flexion / extension | Decrease / increase joint angle |
| Abduction / adduction | Away from / toward midline |
| Rotation | Turning around an axis |
| Circumduction | Cone-shaped movement |
| Pronation / supination | Palm down / palm up |

## High-Yield Pre-Nursing Connections

Synovial joints are where **sprains** (ligament injuries), **dislocations**, **bursitis**, and **arthritis** occur. **Osteoarthritis** is wear of articular cartilage; **rheumatoid arthritis** is autoimmune inflammation of the synovial membrane. Range-of-motion assessment uses the movement terms above, and joint replacements (hip, knee) restore synovial-joint function lost to arthritis. Knowing normal joint anatomy is essential for musculoskeletal assessment and mobility care.

## Common Confusions

- **Structural vs functional classification.** One describes the material connecting bones; the other describes movement. A joint has both labels.
- **Ligament vs tendon.** Ligament = bone to bone (stabilizes joints); tendon = muscle to bone.
- **Flexion vs extension direction.** Flexion decreases the angle (bend); extension increases it (straighten).
- **Cartilage in a joint vs cartilaginous joint.** Synovial joints contain articular cartilage but are not "cartilaginous joints" (which are held together by cartilage and barely move).

## Memory Aids

- **"Synovial = Slippery, freely moving."**
- **Abduction = "Abduct = take away (from midline)."**
- **Flexion = "flex the bicep = bend."**
- **Ball-and-socket = "all-around" motion.**

## ELI-10 Explains

### Simple idea
Joints are the places where bones meet. Some are locked tight, some barely move, and some — the ones full of slippery fluid — move freely so you can bend, twist, and reach.

### Analogy
Think of different kinds of connections in a toy. Some pieces are **glued together** and don't move at all — that's like the **sutures** in your skull (fibrous joints). Some are joined with a bit of **rubber** so they can wiggle a little — like the cushioned joints in your spine (cartilaginous joints). And some are like **well-oiled hinges and ball-joints** that swing freely — those are your **synovial joints**, like your knees, elbows, shoulders, and hips. The freely moving ones come with built-in grease (**synovial fluid**), smooth caps on the bone ends (**cartilage**), and strong straps (**ligaments**) holding them together.

### What is actually happening
Different synovial joints move in different ways: **ball-and-socket** joints (shoulder, hip) swing in all directions, while **hinge** joints (elbow, knee) mainly bend and straighten. The motions have names nurses use — **flexion** (bending), **extension** (straightening), **abduction** (moving away from the middle), and more. Because these moving joints get so much use, they're where injuries like **sprains** and diseases like **arthritis** (worn or inflamed joints) show up.

### Where the analogy stops
Toy hinges wear out and can't fix themselves, but real joints are living — they make fresh lubricating fluid and can heal minor injuries, though badly worn cartilage (arthritis) doesn't grow back well.

## Quick Recap

- Joints are classified **structurally** (fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial) and **functionally** (immovable, slightly movable, freely movable).
- **Synovial joints** (freely movable) have **articular cartilage**, a **capsule** with **synovial fluid**, and **ligaments**; types include ball-and-socket, hinge, pivot, and more.
- Common movements: **flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, rotation, circumduction, pronation/supination**.
- Synovial joints are the main sites of sprains, dislocations, and arthritis.
